newsitem.title: USA: N.Y.S. gov prison bond plan attacked as too costly.
newsitem.headline: N.Y.S. gov prison bond plan attacked as too costly.

text.p: New York State Gov George Pataki's plan to sell $650 million of revenue bonds to pay for new prisons was attacked on Thursday as too costly and unconstitutional, charges Pataki's spokesman disputed.

Daniel Feldman, D-Brooklyn, released a memorandum to him from the state comptroller, who said a financial advisor had calculated that the state could save $94 million by issuing general obligation bonds instead of revenue bonds because they would have a higher rating of A2.

The comparison assumed the proposed revenue bonds would be similar to debt sold by the Empire State Development Corp for correctional facilities, which were rated Baa1 by Moody's Investors Service, the letter added. Feldman said the interest spread between the two bonds would be around 60 basis points.

Both Feldman and the League of Women Voters questioned whether Pataki's plan was permitted under the state's constitution. "The governor's legislative proposal would result in a higher-interest revenue bond format, although there really would be no revenue stream from which to draw. We believe this to be of dubious constitutionality," the League said, in prepared remarks.

The Assemblyman explained that since New York State voters rejected a Prison Construction Bond Issue in a 1981 referendum, new prisons have been financed by what he called revenue-type bonds sold by the Empire State Facilities Development Corp. As the prisons do not make money to pay off the bonds, the legislative appropriates funds for that purpose.

"Anyone who looks at this issue knows that we should not use the financing mechanism the governor has proposed for prison construction, but because we have in fact used this same unjustifiable device for the past 14 years, thus far, silence has prevailed," Feldman said.

Patrick McCarthy, a spokesman for Pataki, said the Assemblyman's proposal to put the issue before the voters was unnecessary, because the governor was elected in part for his tough anti-crime stands, and would could derail the governor's programs that have reduced crime. "What the governor has proposed is completely appropriate and legal."

He added: "This plan (Feldman's) would really be a step away from progress made in the past two years because it fails to keep violent criminals out of our communities and behind bars, where they belong."

The governor's spokesman, reflecting the combative style of Albany politics, did not hesitate to question the Assemblyman's motives, saying Feldman had approved spending over $2.5 billion on new prisons under the former Democratic Administration. Upstate communities, which tend to be Republican strongholds, are expected to request that they get some of the three prisons that Pataki proposed.

The Assembly already has proposed asking voters to approve in November a sale of general obligation bonds for schools, McCarthy said, noting that the state constitution only permits one such ballot proposal a year.
However, another Assembly bill that has been put forward would loosen this curb.

A state source, who declined to be named, said failing to go ahead with Pataki's plan to build three new prisons would cause the state to lose about $75 million in federal aid over the next three years. Albany could not promise its violent felons would serve 85 percent of their sentences--a key condition of getting the aid from Washington--without the new prisons, he explained.
